Educational Objective: Performing a root cause analysis (RCA) involves determining the core systems-level issue that leads to an adverse event such as a patient leaving the hospital without being discharged. Rather than presuming the cause of an adverse event, RCA involves a multidisciplinary team defining and analyzing the problem to design a set of corrective actions based on the analysis. Key Concept: When the underlying cause of an adverse event is unclear, physicians should conduct an RCA of the event to determine the factors contributing to the event. Explanation: RCA involves determining the core systems-level issue(s) that leads to the chain reaction of events that culminate in the adverse event. There are several RCA strategies, including creating a timeline, surveying the controls in place that may have failed, and completing a risk tree analysis where the impact of each event is considered. Regardless of strategy, a typical RCA involves assembling a multidisciplinary team and meeting with this team regularly for a period. This team works to define and analyze the problem to design a set of corrective actions based on the analysis. Differential: This case involved erroneous documentation. Though certain corrective measures may ultimately be taken to prevent future similar events, first the team needs to identify possible systemic causes so that any corrections can be targeted toward the core problem. Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E. Choice A and Choice D: Change the EHR hand-off work flow and provide in-service training on proper work-around documentation are premature. Though certain corrective measures such as these may ultimately be taken to prevent future similar events, first the team needs to identify possible systemic causes so that any corrections can be targeted toward the core problem. Choice B: Notify the hospital attorney is incorrect. Hospital attorneys do not need to be notified about all adverse events. In many hospital systems, internal safety reporting systems should be used and risk managers should be consulted first. Choice E: Suspend the charge nurse is incorrect. Most adverse events are driven by systems-level factors rather than the culpability of individual caregivers. Further, this action makes a premature assumption about the nurse being the cause of the problem without analyzing possible systemic causes.

questions.stem: A Chief of Staff at a hospital is asked to investigate an incident in which a 72-year-old man with diminished mental capacity dressed himself and left the hospital before formal discharge. The next day, the patient was located safe and unharmed 5 miles away. Investigation shows that the search for the patient was delayed because identification-band checking and observation of the patient were documented during a nursing shift change, although these functions were never performed. The patient’s electronic health record (EHR) also indicated that he was observed on the floor, when, in reality, he had left the floor 90 minutes earlier. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial action for the Chief of Staff to take?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: F. Educational Objective: The 5-year-old healthy girl in this case is up-to-date on her vaccines through age 3 years. Administration of the varicella vaccine is the most appropriate next vaccine. Key Concept: Varicella virus infection, or chickenpox, may present with a pruritic, vesicular rash accompanied by fever, malaise, and headache. The varicella virus vaccine is highly effective in preventing chickenpox, especially severe disease, and provides long-lasting immunity. It is routinely recommended for children starting at age 12 months. Explanation: The varicella virus vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine that is normally administered twice as part of the recommended vaccination schedule. The first dose is administered between ages 12 and 15 months and the second dose is administered between ages 4 and 6 years. Previous studies have found that the varicella vaccine, when administered in two doses, is up to 99% effective in decreasing moderate-to-severe disease. For this 5-year-old patient who is up-to-date on her vaccinations, it is most appropriate to administer the second dose of the varicella virus vaccine now. Differential: The varicella vaccine is administered twice during the routine vaccination schedule. This 5-year-old patient is up-to-date on her vaccinations with the last vaccine received at age 3 years, which makes varicella vaccine administration the most appropriate at this time. The other vaccines listed either were already administered earlier in this patient’s life, or should be administered at a later age. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E. Choice A: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) is incorrect. The Hib vaccine is typically administered earlier in life. Depending on the vaccine product used, vaccination against Hib should be completed by age 15 months. Choice B: Hepatitis B is incorrect. Hepatitis B vaccination is routinely given in a three-dose series. The last dose is typically received between age 6 and 18 months. Choice C: Meningococcal is incorrect. The meningococcal vaccine is typically administered twice in older children. The first dose is recommended at age 11 to 12 years with a booster at age 16 years. Choice D: Pneumococcal is incorrect. The pneumococcal vaccine is typically administered over the course of four vaccinations. The last dose is typically given at age 12 to 15 months in a healthy patient. Choice E: Rotavirus is incorrect. The rotavirus vaccine may be administered in a two or three dose regimen. Vaccination against rotavirus is usually completed by age 6 months.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: Addressing this patient’s concern about laryngeal carcinoma requires modifying her risk factors for its development. While there are other health effects associated with her career and caffeine intake, the strongest risk factor she has for laryngeal cancer development is her alcohol use. Thus, the most appropriate recommendation is to decrease her intake of alcohol. Key Concept: The primary risk factors for laryngeal cancer include tobacco and alcohol use and human papillomavirus infection. Explanation: Laryngeal carcinoma may present with hoarseness, vocal changes, persistent cough, stridor, or dysphagia. Most of the laryngeal carcinomas are squamous, and location in the glottic or supraglottic region is common. The diagnosis is established by direct tumor visualization, which may be accomplished by indirect laryngoscopy. Early-stage disease is associated with a high survival rate, although locally extensive or metastatic disease is more difficult to treat. Treatment involves surgical excision, radiotherapy, and/or chemotherapy. Differential: Of this patient’s health habits, the one most significantly associated with laryngeal cancer is alcohol use. While her other habits can have deleterious consequences, they are not directly linked to laryngeal carcinoma. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Changing her work environment is incorrect. Exposure to aerosolized chemicals, inks, and fumes can lead to airway inflammation and bronchitis. Prolonged exposure to specific chemicals can also increase risk for lung cancer. However, this occupation is not associated with an increased risk for laryngeal carcinoma. Choice C: Decreasing her intake of caffeine is incorrect. High caffeine intake can increase the risk for cardiac dysrhythmias, hypertension, tremors, and insomnia. However, excessive consumption of caffeine has not been proven to be a risk factor for laryngeal carcinoma. Choice D: Testing her home for radon is incorrect. Radon exposure has been linked to an increase in rates of lung cancer, but not laryngeal carcinoma. Choice E: No intervention is indicated at this time is incorrect. This patient has expressed concerns about her risk for developing laryngeal cancer, and her health habits do place her at increased risk. Thus, it is pertinent to recommend she decrease her alcohol consumption to decrease her risk.

Educational Objective: Overflow incontinence occurs when bladder emptying is impaired, eventually resulting in intravesical hydrostatic pressure overcoming internal and external urinary sphincter closing pressures, thereby causing the leakage of urine. Common causes include neurologic insults that result in ineffective detrusor muscle contractions, such as diabetic neuropathy or multiple sclerosis (as in this patient’s case), or bladder outlet obstruction. Evaluation: Overflow incontinence occurs when bladder emptying is impaired, eventually resulting in intravesical hydrostatic pressure overcoming internal and external urinary sphincter closing pressures, thereby causing the leakage of urine. It is characterized by chronic urinary retention and bladder distention with increased postvoid residual bladder volume. Definition: Overflow incontinence can occur due to a variety of causes, including neurologic insults (eg, diabetic neuropathy, stroke, trauma, multiple sclerosis) that result in ineffective detrusor muscle contractions, bladder outlet obstruction (eg, benign prostatic hyperplasia, bladder mass, urethral stricture), or as a side effect of some medications (eg, anticholinergics). Patients develop urinary retention with an inability to void completely. They may display loss of urine with Valsalva maneuver or increased abdominopelvic pressure, or the loss of urine may occur randomly. The diagnosis is established with a urodynamic study, which typically displays an increased postvoid residual volume. Prevention: The risk for neurogenic bladder can be mitigated by treatment of inciting conditions. Treatment: Treatment includes management of inciting conditions, timed voiding, and intermittent urinary catheterization. Medications such as bethanechol, a muscarinic agent that promotes bladder contraction, may also be used. Differential: This patient likely has overflow incontinence with passive leakage of urine and a soft, nontender midline mass in the lower abdomen that is likely her overdistended bladder. Her overflow incontinence is likely due to ineffective bladder contractions, or neurogenic bladder secondary to her multiple sclerosis. Neurogenic bladder causing overflow incontinence is a common complication of multiple sclerosis, making it more likely than a mechanical obstruction, while the other options listed are more consistent with stress incontinence or urge incontinence. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choice B and Choice E: Malfunction of the urinary sphincters and relaxation of the pelvic muscles are incorrect. Stress incontinence is incontinence that is triggered by an increase in intra-abdominal pressure (eg, lifting, sneezing, Valsalva maneuver). Stress incontinence results from urethral hypermobility, intrinsic sphincter deficiency, or pelvic floor weakness. Risk factors include multiple vaginal deliveries, obesity, and prostate surgery. Choice C: Mechanical obstruction of urinary flow is incorrect. While bladder outlet obstruction can cause overflow incontinence, neurogenic bladder secondary to her multiple sclerosis is more likely to be the cause. Choice D: Overactivity of the detrusor muscle is incorrect. Overactivity of the detrusor results in urge incontinence, which presents with the urge to void followed shortly by the leakage of urine. Treatments include oxybutynin, an antimuscarinic medication used to treat urge incontinence from an overactive bladder and detrusor instability. This patient does not experience urinary urgency and has an increased postvoid residual volume, which is consistent with overflow incontinence.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: Chronic use of a proton pump inhibitor , such as omeprazole, can cause vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, leading to macrocytic anemia due to impaired gastric acid–dependent absorption. Evaluation: The patient has mild anemia with hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL and an increased mean corpuscular volume of 104.3 µm3, consistent with macrocytic anemia, in the setting of chronic medication use including a proton pump inhibitor. Proton pump inhibitor use can lead to cobalamin deficiency, causing macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia. Definition: Cobalamin deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia characterized by macrocytosis, typically with mean corpuscular volume greater than 100 µm3, due to impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. Gastric acid is required to release cobalamin from dietary proteins, after which it binds intrinsic factor for absorption in the terminal ileum. Long-term proton pump inhibitor use decreases gastric acid production, impairing this process and leading to gradual cobalamin depletion. This results in ineffective erythropoiesis and macrocytic anemia and may also cause neurologic symptoms if prolonged. Recognition is important in patients on chronic acid suppression therapy presenting with macrocytosis. Prevention: Periodic monitoring or supplementation of vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) should be considered in patients on long-term proton pump inhibitor therapy. Treatment: Management involves cyanocobalamin replacement and reassessment of the need for chronic proton pump inhibitor therapy. Differential: Folic acid deficiency also causes macrocytic anemia with mean corpuscular volume greater than 100 µm³ but is more commonly associated with malnutrition or alcohol use rather than medication-induced malabsorption. Anemia of chronic disease typically presents with normocytic or mildly microcytic anemia rather than macrocytosis. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Choice A: Acetaminophen is incorrect. Acetaminophen toxicity affects the liver but does not cause macrocytic anemia. Acetaminophen does not interfere with folic acid or cobalamin absorption. Choice B: Carvedilol is incorrect. β-Adrenergic blockers do not interfere with vitamin absorption or cause macrocytosis. β-Adrenergic blockers can cause bradycardia, light-headedness, or hypotension in overuse. Choice C: Glipizide is incorrect. Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion and do not affect cobalamin concentrations or red blood cell size. Glipizide can cause hypoglycemia, which acutely presents with tremors, diaphoresis, agitation, and altered mental status. Choice D: Lisinopril is incorrect. ACE inhibitors can affect renal function and potassium concentrations but do not cause macrocytic anemia. Lisinopril can otherwise cause cough and angioedema as adverse effects.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This patient presents with facial comedones and acne. Testosterone plays a prominent role in the development of open and closed comedones, and inflammatory papules consistent with acne. Evaluation: Acne commonly presents in teenage and adult patients as open comedones, closed comedones, inflammatory papules, and subcutaneous nodules. Acne most often affects the face but may involve the chest, back, and buttocks. Acne may worsen in women during menstruation and in men who use anabolic steroids. Definition: Acne vulgaris is the result of inflammation of the pilosebaceous unit and is related to increased sebum production, abnormal keratinization, Cutibacterium acnes overgrowth, and associated inflammation. Locally, testosterone increases sebum production, which contributes to clogged pores, bacterial overgrowth, and inflammation which worsen the condition. Prevention: Measures of skin hygiene such as cleansing of the skin to limit sebum accumulation and keratin overgrowth, topical agents such as salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide, and preventive agents such as tretinoin or antibiotics may limit the development of acne. Treatment: Treatment varies by acne subtype but includes salicylic acid cleansers, benzoyl peroxide washes, topical tretinoin, topical or oral antibiotics, systemic retinoids, oral contraceptives, or spironolactone (a testosterone antagonist). questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: This patient with deep venous thrombosis and a urinary tract infection is found to have an increased INR. The most likely cause of her increased INR is ciprofloxacin therapy, which enhances the anticoagulant effect of warfarin. Evaluation: Ciprofloxacin classically potentiates warfarin’s anticoagulant effect, leading to an increased INR. The interaction results from inhibition of warfarin metabolism through cytochrome P450 (CYP450) inhibition. Definition: Many drug interactions are known to cause decreased metabolism of warfarin, especially those that affect vitamin K concentrations or the CYP450 system. Diagnosis of warfarin-associated increased INR due to drug-drug interaction is through clinical history along with laboratory study showing an increased INR in the absence of another compelling cause. Prevention: Increased INR in this case can be prevented by choosing a different antibiotic that does not interact with the metabolism of warfarin or vitamin K. Treatment: Treatment for warfarin-associated increased INR without bleeding includes holding warfarin doses and continuing to monitor INR closely. If the patient has an INR greater than 10.0, oral vitamin K can be given. If the patient develops major bleeding or life-threatening hemorrhage, prothrombin complex concentrate can be administered for rapid reversal of INR. Differential: This patient’s differential is narrow given recent initiation of antibiotics for urinary tract infection along with chronic warfarin therapy with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0. The patient is on ciprofloxacin therapy, which is potentiating the effect of warfarin and causing an increased INR. The other options listed are more likely to decrease INR, not increase, or have limited to no effect on INR. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choice B: Consumption of bananas is incorrect. Bananas have minimal effect on INR as they have low amounts of vitamin K. Choice C: Consumption of cooked spinach is incorrect. Consumption of cooked spinach would decrease INR due to their high vitamin K contents. Choice D: Rifampin therapy is incorrect. Rifampin decreases warfarin’s effect by increasing the metabolism and breakdown of the drug. Choice E: Trazodone therapy is incorrect. Trazodone is not known to increase INR and does not typically interact with warfarin.

Educational Objective: Bell palsy is due to facial nerve abnormality (the right facial nerve in this patient) and will present with upper and lower hemi-facial weakness. It is important to distinguish Bell palsy from a stroke, which will present with additional focal neurologic deficits, including sensory abnormalities, hyperreflexia, aphasia, neglect, and/or limb weakness/numbness. Evaluation: Bell palsy presents with isolated hemifacial weakness that involves the forehead. Generally, weakness of the face will be unaccompanied by any other neurologic deficit, so the presence of additional deficits should prompt consideration of competing diagnoses. Definition: Bell palsy is isolated dysfunction of the facial nerve, causing complete hemi-facial weakness. Bell palsy may be secondary to reactivation of herpes simplex virus, although may also be idiopathic. Involvement of the forehead strongly suggests a peripheral nerve process as opposed to a stroke, which would cause an upper motor neuron pattern of facial weakness, sparing the muscles of the forehead. Prevention: There is no known prevention of Bell palsy. Treatment: Bell palsy is typically a benign condition that gradually improves over time, although treatment with oral corticosteroids and/or antivirals may expedite recovery. Eye patching and artificial tears should be prescribed to prevent keratitis. Differential: Acute hemi-facial weakness involving the forehead is consistent with Bell palsy, which involves the peripheral cranial seventh nerve and spares central nervous system structures. Abnormalities of the other structures listed would present with additional symptoms not seen in this patient. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, E, and F. Choice A: Left cerebral cortex is incorrect. Lesions involving the left cerebral cortex would cause a broad constellation of signs/symptoms including contralateral leg and arm weakness, numbness, aphasia, dysphagia, visual disturbances, and deficits in executive function. This patient lacks any such issue. Choice B: Left middle cerebral artery is incorrect. Occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery causes left middle cerebral artery syndrome, which is characterized by aphasia, dysphagia, contralateral hand and face weakness/numbness, and contralateral homonymous hemianopsia. Choice C: Left subarachnoid space is incorrect. Rupture of an aneurysm of an artery that makes up the circle of Willis can cause bleeding in the subarachnoid space, also known as a subarachnoid hemorrhage. This classically presents with a sudden, “thunderclap” headache in the absence of new focal neurologic deficits. Choice E: Right frontal lobe is incorrect. Right frontal lobe damage would present with executive function deficits and eye deviation. Choice F: Right sphenoid sinus is incorrect. Damage to the right sphenoid sinus can cause headaches and endocrine imbalances if the damage extends to the sella turcica.

Educational Objective: This patient presents with a 6-month history of cramping pain in his thighs after walking short distances and two myocardial infarctions in the past 5 years, a presentation suggestive of atherosclerotic vascular disease. Prior to aortofemoral reconstruction, he requires pharmacologic stress echocardiography for assessment of cardiac function. Evaluation: Coronary atherosclerosis classically presents as a chronic, progressive cardiovascular disease. It results from the accumulation of lipid-rich plaques in the coronary arteries. It is important that patients are screened preoperatively for risk of coronary ischemia. Definition: While the gold standard for diagnosis of coronary atherosclerosis is coronary angiography, this patient needs both an evaluation of his coronary arteries and of his cardiac function. By starting with a pharmacologic stress echocardiography, both cardiac structure and function can be assessed. If any concern for ischemia is detected on the stress echocardiography, the patient should be referred for coronary angiography. Prevention: Progression of coronary artery disease can be prevented by treating risk factors such as hyperlipidemia and by maintaining a heart-healthy diet and exercise regimen. Treatment: Treatment for coronary atherosclerosis involves optimal pharmacotherapy, including a high-intensity statin and daily aspirin to lower LDL-cholesterol concentrations, stabilize plaque progression, reduce inflammation, and prevent clotting. Differential: This patient has severe vascular disease that requires cardiac function assessment prior to surgery. Evaluation should be focused on assessment of cardiac structure, function, and inducible ischemia. Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E. Choice A: An exercise stress test is impractical; this patient is unable to exercise adequately due to leg claudication. Choice B: 24-Hour ambulatory ECG monitoring is incorrect. 24-Hour ambulatory ECG monitoring would be more useful for assessment of palpitations or intermittent symptoms, which this patient does not have. Choice D: Coronary angiography is incorrect. Although coronary angiography may be necessary prior to surgery, it is most appropriate to start with pharmacologic stress echocardiography to assess cardiac structure and function. If results of pharmacologic stress echocardiography conclude there is a high ischemic burden, coronary angiography would then be appropriate. Choice E: Pulmonary artery catheterization is incorrect. Pulmonary artery catheterization provides hemodynamic variables related to volume status, but it is not indicated in a routine, preoperative ischemia workup.

The most appropriate follow-up testing for this patient is colonoscopy in 3 years. Key Concept: Tubular adenomas are benign neoplastic polyps that are considered high risk when greater than or equal to 1 cm, as well as if villous or high-grade dysplasia findings are identified on pathology examination. Explanation: The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends routine colorectal cancer screening for all patients beginning at age 45 years and continuing until age 75 years. Colorectal cancer is common, and early detection and treatment have been demonstrated to decrease morbidity and mortality. Colonoscopy remains the gold standard screening test as it allows direct visualization and excision of polyps throughout the length of the colon. Tubular adenomas are benign polyps but carry malignant potential. It is recommended that patients with low-risk polyps, such as one or two small (less than 1 cm) tubular adenomas, undergo screening with colonoscopy every 5 to 10 years. Patients with multiple polyps (three or more), polyps with atypical features or large size (greater than or equal to 1 cm), or atypical serrated polyps should undergo more frequent screening every 3 years. Differential: This patient was found to have a single large polyp consistent with tubular adenoma. Due to the 1-cm size of the polyp, it is recommended the patient undergo repeat colonoscopy in 3 years. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and F. Choice A: Annual test of the stool for occult blood is incorrect. It is generally not recommended to test the stool for occult blood for 5 years after a colonoscopy. The findings of a 1-cm polyp in this patient make colonoscopy in 3 years the most appropriate follow-up test. Choice B: Serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) assay now is incorrect. A CEA assay may be considered if colonoscopy identifies invasive colorectal cancer. The CEA assay serves as a baseline for post-treatment surveillance. Choice C: Air-contrast barium enema in 3 years is incorrect. Air-contrast barium enema is no longer recommended for use in colon cancer screening. A repeat colonoscopy in 3 years is more appropriate. Choice D: CT scan of the abdomen now is incorrect. A CT scan may be indicated if there were findings of invasive adenocarcinoma. The findings of a single 1-cm polyp make the recommendation for repeat colonoscopy in 3 years more appropriate. Choice F: No additional testing indicated is incorrect. The patient in this case was found to have a polyp that is 1 cm in size. Based on the size alone of the polyp, the patient should undergo repeat colonoscopy in 3 years.

Educational Objective: Number needed to treat (NNT) is the number of patients that would need to receive a given therapy for one patient to benefit, or 1 / absolute risk reduction (ARR). Since ARR is baseline risk multiplied by the relative risk reduction (RRR), the 50% vaccine RRR multiplied by the baseline risk for 33% is 0.33 × 0.50 = 0.166, and 1 / 0.166 = 6. Key Concept: The NNT is the number of people who would need to be treated for one person to benefit, calculated as 1 / ARR. Explanation: The benefit of some medical interventions can be unclear. The NNT is an easy-to-understand statistic that calculates the number of people who would need to receive the treatment for one person to benefit. NNT is calculated by taking the inverse of the ARR of a given medical intervention. In this case, the RRR is converted to ARR by baseline risk × RRR = ARR. Differential: Given the RRR is 50% and the base rate is 33%, this makes the ARR 0.33 × 0.50 = 0.166; then the NNT is 1 / 0.166 = 6. The other answer choices do not correctly calculate the NNT. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. Choice A: 2 is incorrect. If the ARR were 50%, the NNT would be 2, but the NNT is one over the ARR, not the RRR, which is 50%. Choice B: 3 is incorrect. The base incidence of infection is 33% (absolute risk). The NNT is calculated using the ARR, not the lifetime incidence. Choice C: 4 is incorrect. The NNT is equal to 1 / ARR, which is not correctly calculated here. Choice E: 12 is incorrect. The NNT is equal to 1 / ARR, which is not correctly calculated here.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: Menopause is the most likely cause of this 47-year-old patient’s amenorrhea. In addition to her age and previously regular cycle, her relatively low concentration of estradiol and increased concentrations of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) confirm the diagnosis. Evaluation: Menopause often presents in patients aged around 50 years with amenorrhea, hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal atrophy or dryness. Mood and sleeping patterns may also be affected. Definition: Menopause refers to the absence of menstruation for 1 year due to a diminution in ovarian reserve. In response to the decreased estradiol production from the ovaries, FSH and LH lack negative feedback and are increased in the serum. Menopause is often a clinical diagnosis, but these laboratory values may be obtained if the diagnosis is unclear. Prevention: Menopause reflects normal physiology and cannot be prevented. Treatment: Symptoms of menopause can be treated with hormonal replacement therapy, including supplemental estrogen, but risks for endometrial cancer, thromboembolism, breast cancer, and cardiovascular disease must be weighed against the benefits. Differential: Amenorrhea has many causes. However, the causes that increase FSH and LH in this case are menopause and premature ovarian failure. Premature ovarian failure refers to patients younger than 40 years, which does not apply in this case. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, E, and F. Choice A: Hypothalamic amenorrhea is incorrect. Hypothalamic amenorrhea results from a deficiency of gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion. This consequently decreases FSH and LH concentrations, which are not seen in this patient. Choice C: Pituitary adenoma is incorrect. Pituitary adenomas, primarily prolactinomas, may result in amenorrhea. Increased concentrations of prolactin can decrease the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which also decreases the release of FSH and LH. This patient has normal prolactin concentrations and increased, not decreased, FSH and LH concentrations. Choice D: Polycystic ovarian syndrome is incorrect. Polycystic ovarian syndrome, now known as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, classically causes amenorrhea secondary to anovulation. Other presenting features may include signs of androgen excess (eg, hirsutism), obesity, insulin resistance, and polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasonography. Choice E: Pregnancy is incorrect. Pregnancy is an important cause of amenorrhea in patients of reproductive age and should be appropriately ruled out. In pregnancy, estradiol and progesterone are increased, causing negative feedback on the release of FSH and LH. These hormone changes are not seen in this patient. Choice F: Premature ovarian failure is incorrect. While premature ovarian failure presents similarly to menopause due to atresia of the ovarian follicles and decrease in estradiol, it is a term reserved for patients younger than 40 years. This patient is 47 years old, and menopause is the more fitting diagnosis.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: Herpes simplex infection, also called herpetic whitlow, is the most likely cause of this patient’s painful cluster of vesicles on an erythematous base involving the distal left index finger. Evaluation: Herpetic whitlow is a clinical diagnosis and presents with painful erythema and vesicular lesions on a distal finger or toe. Patients often have an exposure to herpesvirus 1 or herpesvirus 2 prior to development of symptoms. Initially, patients may experience a prodromal tingling or burning pain at the site of involvement. Definition: Herpetic whitlow represents a localized herpesvirus infection following exposure to the herpesvirus 1 or herpesvirus 2. Common potential exposures include oral or genital herpetic lesions. Dentists and dental hygienists are often affected. In cases where the diagnosis is uncertain, herpesvirus polymerase chain reaction testing can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. Prevention: Patients may prevent development of herpetic whitlow by avoidance of contact with individuals who have an active herpesvirus infection. Treatment: Patients with herpetic whitlow may benefit from treatment with an oral antiviral including acyclovir or valacyclovir. Pain control should be offered as well, and neuromodulatory agents such as gabapentin may offer additional relief. Differential: In this patient with development of painful, vesicular lesions of the left index finger following exposure to an oral infection, the most likely diagnosis is herpetic whitlow. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choice B: Pasteurella infection is incorrect. Pasteurella species infection is commonly associated with dog or cat bites; this patient’s lesions are vesicles, not punctures. Recommended treatment to prevent Pasteurella species infection after a bite includes thorough irrigation of the area as well as initiation of oral antibiotics, commonly amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. Choice C: Staphylococcus aureus abscess is incorrect. S aureus abscesses typically present as painful, erythematous, subcutaneous nodules with overlying comedones. Abscesses may be treated with incision and drainage followed by oral antibiotics. This patient's condition is consistent with herpetic whitlow, as opposed to an abscess. Choice D: Streptococcal cellulitis is incorrect. Streptococcal cellulitis presents with a well demarcated, erythematous and indurated expanding cutaneous patch or plaque. Streptococcal cellulitis often starts with an initial inoculation via trauma or skin breakdown followed by subsequent soft tissue infection. Bacterial cellulitis is treated with antibiotics. Choice E: Tinea corporis is incorrect. Tinea corporis is a superficial fungal infection that clinically presents with an erythematous ring-shaped plaque with peripheral scale. Tinea corporis is treated with topical or oral antifungals.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: This patient presents with multiple symptoms and signs of anorexia nervosa. Patients with anorexia nervosa are at risk for cardiac arrhythmias due to electrolyte abnormalities and sometimes as a side effect of medications used for weight loss. Evaluation: Patients with anorexia nervosa generally present with low BMI, limited intake of food, and increased activities to compensate for caloric intake such as excess exercise or induced vomiting. Amenorrhea is also a common presenting symptom. Patients with anorexia nervosa often have a BMI less than 17 kg/m2. Definition: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by an intense fear of gaining weight, decreased self-worth related to body weight, and consequent restricting (eg, fasting, exercising) or binge eating/purging behavior (eg, vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse) leading to insufficient nutrition. Physical examination of patients with anorexia nervosa can show dry, scaly skin and fine hair or hair loss due to decreased protein stores. Severe malnutrition can lead to amenorrhea, constipation (secondary to dehydration, decreased gut motility, and electrolyte imbalances), and parasympathetic activation to conserve energy (manifesting as bradycardia, hypotension). Patients with anorexia nervosa are at increased risk for cardiac arrhythmia due to electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia in setting of starvation), autonomic abnormalities, and cardiac atrophy secondary to starvation, among other factors. Prevention: Interventions that promote healthy body image and eating habits may help prevent anorexia nervosa. Treatment: Treatment of anorexia nervosa is through a combined medical and psychiatric approach and involves correcting fluid and electrolyte derangements along with behavioral therapy. Differential: This patient’s presenting symptoms are most consistent with anorexia nervosa. Of the other options listed, Cushing disease is associated with weight gain, and rheumatoid arthritis would be expected to have joint pain and swelling as the presenting symptoms, making them less likely. Graves disease and lymphoma may both be associated with weight loss, but they also present with additional systemic findings not seen in this patient. Gastrointestinal disorders causing decreased oral intake should also be excluded. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choice B: Cushing disease is incorrect. Cushing disease, caused by excess cortisol, leads to lipogenic conditions, presenting with weight gain, central obesity, and round facies rather than weight loss. Choice C: Graves disease is incorrect. While hyperthyroidism is associated with weight loss, excessive thyroid hormone leads to tachycardia and hypertension rather than bradycardia and hypotension. As well, constipation and amenorrhea are more consistent with anorexia nervosa. Choice D: Lymphoma is incorrect. While lymphoma and other malignancies are associated with weight loss, patients typically present with other B symptoms (fever, night sweats) along with lymphadenopathy. As well, constipation and amenorrhea are more consistent with anorexia nervosa. Choice E: Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. This patient does not present with joint pain or swelling. Weight loss is not classically associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: Severe pain, swelling, and erythema in the great toe after consuming a large amount of alcohol or purines is consistent with gout. The most likely diagnosis in this patient’s case is gout, making oral colchicine the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for the patient. Evaluation: Gout may present with a warm, tender joint often with a palpable effusion or overlying edema. Definition: Gout classically presents following consumption of a purine-rich meal, especially red meat or seafood, often in males aged between 30 and 70 years. Other risk factors for gout flares include trauma, surgery, dehydration, or use of thiazide or loop diuretics. As uric acid accumulates, it crystallizes and precipitates in synovial fluid which is identified as negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals on microscopy. The crystals trigger an inflammatory reaction in the joint characterized by the infiltration of leukocytes with resultant production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. Prevention: Gout flares may be avoided with dietary modifications and avoidance of thiazide or loop diuretics. Treatment: The preferred treatment of a gout flare is NSAIDs, oral corticosteroids, or colchicine, due to its anti-inflammatory effects. Allopurinol may be used to decrease the risk for disease recurrence. Differential: This 52-year-old man has risk factors for gout including recent large consumption of alcohol and use of a thiazide medication. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient during his acute gout flare is oral colchicine. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Oral allopurinol is incorrect. Allopurinol is an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, the enzyme responsible for the final step in metabolism of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid. Excess uric acid can precipitate in joints leading to the development of acute gout. Allopurinol is an important agent in decreasing the risk for developing a gout flare. It does not have anti-inflammatory properties and will not reduce pain or swelling in an acute gout flare. Choice C: Oral methotrexate is incorrect. Methotrexate therapy is a corticosteroid-sparing treatment for autoimmune and autoinflammatory conditions, such as psoriasis. Methotrexate inhibits the function of dihydrofolate reductase, preventing the production of thymidine required for DNA synthesis. Choice D: Oral methylprednisolone is incorrect. Oral corticosteroids may be used in cases of acute gout flares. In this case, colchicine may be the more appropriate pharmacotherapy as the patient has had partial relief with ibuprofen previously. Choice E: Intramuscular ceftriaxone is incorrect. Ceftriaxone therapy is used in the treatment of a variety of infections, such as community-acquired pneumonia, bacterial meningitis, and acute otitis media. Ceftriaxone therapy is not used in cases of acute gout flares.

Educational Objective: In this case, the primary change is the means of communication, which transitioned from indirect, asynchronous communication via the electronic health record to live, direct conversation. Live conversation allows for more effective communication through immediate clarification and feedback and a shared mental model. Key Concept: Communication about patient care should ideally occur via live conversation with the relevant team members present. Often, the patient is a relevant team member who can enhance the history and assist the team in targeting discussion of the assessment and plan to the patient’s priorities who can provide corrections and clarifications and ask questions in real time to enhance their understanding. Explanation: In live conversations, team members can provide clarifications and feedback in real time to improve mutual understanding in the form of a shared mental model of the patient’s situation. Live conversations are thus a cornerstone of interprofessional collaboration. Alternatively, asynchronous communication limits the reciprocal flow of information and can increase the chance of misunderstanding. Differential: Including the patient in team conversations can improve patient engagement and promote mutual trust and shared goals. However, these are considered secondary outcomes. The physician’s intervention more specifically targets staff communication methods. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Clear roles is incorrect. The roles of the medical assistant and physician remain stable, though the method of communication improves. Choice C: Measurable processes and outcomes is incorrect. Educational Objective: Primary hyperparathyroidism should be suspected in patients with hypercalcemia and nephrolithiasis and is confirmed by an inappropriately increased parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration. Evaluation: The patient presents after a first kidney stone and is found to have mild hypercalcemia with serum calcium 10.8 mg/dL, which is above the normal range, raising concern for an underlying metabolic cause of nephrolithiasis. Definition: Primary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by autonomous overproduction of PTH, leading to increased bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and increased intestinal calcium absorption via activation of vitamin D. The result is hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia, with complications including nephrolithiasis due to hypercalciuria. The key diagnostic feature is an inappropriately normal or increased PTH concentration in the setting of hypercalcemia, as normal physiology would suppress PTH when calcium exceeds 10.5 mg/dL. This distinction confirms PTH-mediated hypercalcemia and differentiates it from other causes such as malignancy, where PTH is suppressed. Prevention: Adequate hydration and management of hypercalcemia decrease the risk for recurrent nephrolithiasis. There is no specific prevention for primary hyperparathyroidism. Treatment: Definitive treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism is parathyroidectomy in symptomatic patients or those meeting criteria, including nephrolithiasis or serum calcium more than 1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal. Differential: Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia presents with increased calcium and suppressed PTH, often with more severe hypercalcemia and systemic symptoms. Vitamin D–mediated hypercalcemia causes increased calcium with vitamin D metabolites but also suppresses PTH. In this case, the increased calcium concentration and lack of any other electrolyte imbalances or systemic symptoms argues for primary hyperparathyroidism. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. Choice A and Choice B: Calcitriol and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D are incorrect. Increased calcitriol concentrations are seen in granulomatous diseases, Vitamin D-mediated hypercalcemia, and some lymphomas but do not confirm primary hyperparathyroidism. Similarly, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is increased in vitamin D-mediated hypercalcemia and would be associated with suppressed PTH rather than confirming a PTH-driven process. Choice C: Magnesium is incorrect. Magnesium abnormalities can affect PTH secretion but do not confirm the diagnosis of hyperparathyroidism. Choice E: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is incorrect. Thyroid dysfunction does not explain hypercalcemia with nephrolithiasis and is not part of the diagnostic evaluation for suspected hyperparathyroidism.

Educational Objective: The most appropriate next step in evaluation of this 13-year-old patient’s health risks is to ask the father to leave the room and continue obtaining patient history. Providing a confidential environment for the patient may encourage her to ask questions or provide information that she is not comfortable discussing in front of her parent, allowing for a more complete evaluation of potential health risks. Key Concept: It is generally recommended to begin having personal one-on-one time with pediatric patients beginning around ages 11 to 13 years. Preteens and teenagers may have questions or information to provide which they don’t feel comfortable discussing in front of a parent. Explanation: Having the ability to have a private conversation with a pediatric patient is important to gain patient trust and discuss sensitive topics. It has been found that when pediatric patients do not have a confidential environment in which to speak, they are less likely to disclose substance use, pursue sexually transmitted infection screening, or ask about contraceptive services. It is important to discuss the limitations of confidentiality when speaking to pediatric patients and informing parents of the importance of the confidential time. Differential: This 13-year-old patient presents for a routine health maintenance examination and has no concerning symptoms or health concerns at this time. Calculating the patient’s BMI, determining blood pressure percentage, and reviewing for missed vaccinations are also reasonable at this visit, but can be completed after obtaining the patient’s full history. Asking the father to leave the room and continuing to obtain patient history would be the most appropriate immediate next step in evaluation of this patient’s health risks. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choice B: Calculate the patient’s BMI is incorrect. Calculating a patient’s BMI is important to monitor for disordered eating or high BMI so patients can be referred for behavioral interventions. Having a confidential conversation with the patient would be more appropriate in this case. Choice C: Contact the patient’s mother for collateral history is incorrect. Contacting the patient’s mother may be a reasonable answer choice if there is history that is unable to be provided by the patient or her father. Creating a space for a confidential conversation with the patient would be more appropriate. Choice D: Determine blood pressure percentile by age and stature is incorrect. Monitoring for hypertension is recommended in pediatric patients. However, it would be most appropriate to first obtain a complete patient history, which can be achieved by asking the father to leave the room to allow for a confidential conversation. Choice E: Review the state immunization database for missing vaccinations is incorrect. It is generally recommended to review the state immunization database at patient visits to evaluate for missing vaccinations. However, delaying this review to later in the visit poses no immediate risk to the patient. In this case, having a private and confidential conversation with the patient first would better help to evaluate her health risks.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This patient initially presented with and was treated for a pulmonary embolism and is now asymptomatic. Despite resolution of her symptoms, the most appropriate next step in management is warfarin therapy for 6 months to reduce the risk of recurrence. Evaluation: Pulmonary embolism presents with acute pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, tachycardia, and hypoxia, often in a patient with deep venous thrombosis or a known hypercoagulable state. Hypotension, syncope, right ventricular failure, and cardiovascular collapse may occur with large pulmonary emboli. Definition: Pulmonary thromboembolism is a common disorder caused by occlusion of a pulmonary artery and impaired blood flow to a segment of the lungs. Risk factors include immobility, obesity, recent surgery, pregnancy, use of combination oral contraceptives, smoking, trauma, fracture of long bones, and inherited or acquired hypercoagulable disorders. Diagnosis is most commonly made with CT angiography of the pulmonary vessels. Prevention: Prevention depends on patient risk factors. For example, in patients with impaired mobility (eg, postoperative or hospitalized patients) or in hypercoagulable states, prophylactic treatment with blood thinners is common. Treatment: Treatment depends on the size of the pulmonary embolism and the patient’s symptoms. For initial low-risk pulmonary emboli—in which there is no associated hemodynamic compromise and no significant systemic or cardiopulmonary disease—treatment with blood-thinning agents such as warfarin for 6 months is standard. Differential: Neither aspirin therapy nor the use of bilateral knee-length compressing stockings are sufficient treatment of pulmonary emboli. Low-molecular weight heparin would be an appropriate treatment, but 1 month is too short in duration. Five years of warfarin therapy is too long in duration. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and F. Choice A and Choice B: Aspirin therapy for 1 month and aspirin therapy for 6 months are incorrect. Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent used in the treatment of coronary artery disease and peripheral artery disease, especially after procedural intervention. Aspirin does not cause sufficient anticoagulation to treat pulmonary embolism. Choice C: Low-molecular-weight heparin therapy for 1 month is incorrect. While low-molecular-weight heparin can be used in the treatment of pulmonary embolism, patients often prefer oral anticoagulants to this injectable medication. Furthermore, 1 month of therapy is an inadequate amount of time to treat a pulmonary embolism and prevent further complications. Choice D: Use of bilateral knee-length compression stockings for 5 months is incorrect. Use of bilateral knee-length compression stockings is associated with a decreased risk for lower extremity deep venous thrombosis, often the precursor to pulmonary emboli. However, they do not play a role in treating pulmonary emboli. Choice F: Warfarin therapy for 5 years is incorrect. Warfarin would be an appropriate anticoagulation for this patient. However, warfarin therapy for 5 years would increase the risk for complications (eg, bleeding) with no added benefit over treatment for 6 months.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: The predictive value of a positive test, or positive predictive value (PPV), is the percent of patients with a positive test who are true positive (TP) (having the disease in question). The vignette describes a relatively low number of men with occult blood in their stools that go on to be diagnosed with colon cancer, illustrating the poor PPV of occult blood screening tests. Key Concept: Given a positive test, the PPV is the percent likelihood the positive test represents a TP and is generally low in screening tests. Explanation: PPV and negative predictive value (NPV) are statistical measures of the proportion of positive and negative test results that are TPs and true negatives (TN), respectively. PPV measures the probability of a patient having the tested for disease given a positive test result, and NPV measures the probability of a patient being disease-free given a negative test result. PPV is calculated as TP / (TP + false positive [FP]), and NPV is calculated as TN / (TN + false negative). PPV varies directly with disease prevalence, whereas NPV varies inversely with disease prevalence. Since screening tests attempt to identify all potential incidences of a disease using low thresholds, they usually result in a high number of FPs and consequentially a low PPV. Differential: The vignette outlines the number of TP men for colon cancer given a much larger number of individuals testing positive for occult blood, which is the predictive value of a positive test. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, E, and F. Choice A: False-positive rate is incorrect. In this case, 76 men tested positive but did not have colon cancer; 76/88 represents the false-positive rate. Choice B: Likelihood ratio is incorrect. Likelihood ratios quantify the change in disease probability between pretest and post-test probability. In this case, the PPV is being assessed. Choice C: Predictive value of a negative test is incorrect. In this case, the statistic in question involves those who tested positive for the screening test, not negative. Choice E: Sensitivity is incorrect. Sensitivity is TP / TP + false negative, and while screening tests tend to be sensitive, sensitivity is not being tested in this example. Choice F: Specificity is incorrect. Specificity is TN / TN + FP, and while screening tests tend to be poorly specific, specificity is not being tested in this example.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: This patient’s presentation is consistent with acute pyelonephritis, a urinary tract infection (UTI) that has spread to the kidneys. It is characterized by flank pain, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, and costovertebral tenderness on physical examination. Urinalysis may show positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, leukocytes, red blood cells, and white blood cell casts. Evaluation: Presentation of pyelonephritis includes flank pain, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, and costovertebral tenderness on physical examination. Urinalysis typically shows positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites and WBCs greater than 10/hpf. Urinalysis may show red cells as evidence of mucosal inflammation (or concomitant nephrolithiasis) and may show white blood cell casts. Bacteria are generally seen on microscopy, with gram-negative rods being the most common pathogen. Urine may be dark colored or foul smelling. Definition: Pyelonephritis is an infection of the kidney that commonly results from retrograde spread of a lower UTI. UTIs are more common in women due to the shorter urethra and favorable regional environment for bacterial growth. If untreated, bacteria can travel up the ureter to infect the kidney, resulting in pyelonephritis. Prevention: Because it results from the spread of infection from the lower urinary tract, prompt diagnosis and treatment of UTIs is necessary to prevent pyelonephritis. Lower UTIs present with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. Treatment: UTIs are most commonly caused by Escherichia coli and gram-negative enteric flora, but some gram-positive organisms may be the culprit. Antibiotic choice should be tailored to microbial sensitivities while ensuring that the selected agent is the appropriate strength for the infection. In the case of pyelonephritis, a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, or an oral β-lactam (amoxicillin/clavulanate, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime) should be given. Care should be taken to avoid side effects that may be damaging to a patient (eg, hearing loss from aminoglycoside antibiotics) when possible. Differential: This patient’s systemic infectious symptoms, evidence of UTI on urinalysis, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness are most consistent with pyelonephritis. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Cystitis is incorrect. Lower UTI symptoms include dysuria, frequency, urgency, incontinence, and suprapubic pain. Urinalysis will typically show bacteriuria, white blood cells, positive leukocyte esterase, and positive nitrites depending on the infectious organism. Though this patient’s urinalysis is similar, the presence of flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness is more consistent with pyelonephritis. Additionally, localized cystitis is unlikely to cause systemic infectious signs with fever. Choice C: Renal calculi is incorrect. Nephrolithiasis presents with colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, gross hematuria, and difficulty voiding. A concomitant UTI may or may not be present. While superinfection of a renal stone is one of the causes of pyelonephritis, this patient’s history does not display any evidence of nephrolithiasis and retrograde spread of a lower UTI is a more common cause. questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: This patient presents with a recent history of drug-eluting stent placement in the left anterior descending coronary artery. Following stent placement, it is imperative that patients receive dual antiplatelet therapy to prevent in-stent restenosis (ISR). In addition to continued aspirin therapy, a 1-year course of clopidogrel is indicated for this patient. Evaluation: ISR classically presents with recurrent angina, arm pain, jaw pain, or shortness of breath after stent placement, generally within days if acute or after weeks to months if slowly progressive or a chronic reocclusion. Definition: ISR is the result of neointimal hyperplasia at the site of a previously placed stent. It most commonly occurs within 6 months post-stent placement and typically presents as a return of the patient’s original symptoms (eg, angina). Diagnosis of ISR is confirmed by coronary angiography or advanced cardiac imaging that shows narrowing of the coronary vessel at the location of the prior stent. Prevention: ISR can be prevented by adherence to a dual antiplatelet regimen, which includes aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel. Prevention of ISR is critical for stabilizing the coronary artery and decreasing the likelihood of acute coronary syndromes, morbidity, and mortality. Treatment: If stenosis were to occur, treatment for ISR can include medical management or interventional cardiology procedures (sometimes more layers of stents) to reopen the affected blood vessel. Differential: This patient’s differential is narrow given his known recent coronary stent placement and current aspirin use. Prevention of coronary stent restenosis is through compliance with a dual antiplatelet therapy regimen. A 1-year course of a P2Y12 inhibitor, such as clopidogrel, is indicated to prevent restenosis of this patient’s left anterior descending coronary artery. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choices B, C, and E: Dabigatran, enoxaparin, and warfarin are incorrect. These medications are anticoagulants, which do not target neointimal growth and are not the primary treatment for ISR. Treatment with anticoagulants in conjunction with P2Y12 inhibitors may be considered for patients with comorbidities, such as atrial fibrillation, to reduce the risk of thrombotic events. Choice D: Metoprolol is incorrect. Metoprolol is a cardioselective β1-adrenergic blocker that can be used as an antianginal medication. It has no direct effect on vascular smooth muscle proliferation and thus does not prevent ISR.

Educational Objective: This 15-year-old female presents with heavy menstrual periods and fatigue and is likely experiencing iron deficiency leading to anemia. Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) in teenage girls can occur in the setting of heavy menstrual bleeding. Evaluation: IDA classically presents with fatigue and pallor. In extreme cases, it can present with dyspnea on exertion, light-headedness, tachycardia, hypotension, and lactic acidosis. Definition: IDA results from iron losses, such as through menses, which exceed intake and lead to inadequate iron availability for hemoglobin synthesis and developing red blood cells. Iron deficiency leads to microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells and decreased production, which results in anemia. The gold standard for diagnosis of IDA is low serum ferritin concentrations and serum iron concentrations plus complete blood count indices. Supporting evidence includes clinical history. Prevention: IDA can be prevented by dietary counseling to increase iron intake and avoiding iron absorption inhibitors. Additional prevention strategies include annual screening for high-risk adolescents, prophylactic iron supplementation, and management of heavy menstrual bleeding with hormonal therapies when appropriate. Treatment: Treatment for IDA includes oral iron supplementation combined with dietary counseling and management of underlying heavy menstrual bleeding. Differential: This patient’s differential is initially broad regarding her cause of fatigue and heavy menstruation. Diagnoses such as a bleeding disorder or hormonal imbalances can impact the level of menstruation this patient is experiencing. However, her symptoms are likely driven by nutritional deficiency in the setting of increased iron loss. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A and Choice E: Folic acid and vitamin B12 (cobalamin) are incorrect. While folic acid and vitamin B12 deficiency can cause anemia and fatigue, the clinical history of heavy menses in an otherwise healthy teenager is more consistent with IDA. Choice C: Progesterone is incorrect. Progesterone deficiency would result in symptoms such as infertility. Choice D: Thyroid-stimulating hormone is incorrect. While hypothyroidism may cause fatigue, it is less likely as this patient has a normal physical examination otherwise and a compelling history for IDA in the setting of heavy menstrual cycles.

Educational Objective: Osteoporosis is a common condition that is characterized by the progressive loss of bone mineral density, leading to decreased bone strength. Cessation of smoking would provide the greatest decrease in this patient’s risk for osteoporosis, as cigarette smoking is associated with accelerated bone loss. Evaluation: Osteoporosis is usually asymptomatic but may present with a fracture often involving the hip, vertebrae, or distal radius. Risk can be assessed with bone density studies. Definition: Osteoporosis classically affects patients who are postmenopausal with inflammatory disorders, and individuals with metabolic or endocrine disorders such as hypercortisolism or with long-term corticosteroid use. Decreased bone mineral density can lead to fragility fractures, which can greatly decrease mobility and even increase the risk of death in older individuals. Cigarette smoking has been associated with accelerated bone loss and an increased risk for fractures and osteoporosis. Prevention: Common risk factors for the development of osteoporosis include smoking, age, chronic inflammatory disease, corticosteroid use, and estrogen-depleting conditions in women, which may be exacerbated by smoking. Treatment: Calcium and vitamin D are the supplementations of choice for treatment and prevention of osteoporosis. In addition to vitamin supplementation, bisphosphonates such as alendronate are typically the first-line medications used in osteoporosis to prevent further loss of bone density. Differential: The patient in this case is a long-term cigarette smoker, currently smoking one pack of cigarettes daily. Cessation of smoking is a key modifiable risk factor contributing to the development of osteoporosis and would provide the greatest decrease in this patient’s risk. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Cessation of alcohol use is incorrect. Alcohol use has been associated with an increased risk for osteoporosis, especially when consuming more than two alcoholic beverages daily. Cigarette smoking has been associated with a higher risk for developing osteoporosis. Choice C: Fluoride supplementation is incorrect. Fluoride supplementation has not been found to decrease the risk for developing osteoporosis. Cessation of smoking would best decrease this patient’s risk for osteoporosis. Choice D and Choice E: Increase in calcium intake and vitamin D supplementation are incorrect. Calcium and vitamin D are the supplementations of choice for treatment and prevention of osteoporosis. However, cigarette smoking cessation has been found to have a greater effect on decreasing the risk for the development of osteoporosis.

Educational Objective: Pediatric patients with obesity and additional risk factors such as family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus should undergo targeted screening for hyperglycemia, even when presenting for unrelated symptoms. For this patient, measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration is appropriate at this time. Evaluation: The patient has exertional cough and wheezing consistent with exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, but the key additional finding is obesity with BMI 31 kg/m2 and a first-degree family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, which places him at increased risk for insulin resistance. Definition: Impaired fasting glucose is a prediabetic state defined by fasting plasma glucose between 100 and 125 mg/dL, reflecting early insulin resistance and β-cell dysfunction. In children, obesity is the primary driver, especially when combined with a family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Although there is no recommendation for universal screening in asymptomatic children, high-risk patients should be screened using a risk-based approach. This includes children aged 10 years or older, or at the onset of puberty, who are overweight or obese, defined as BMI at or above the 85th percentile, and who have at least one additional risk factor such as family history. This patient meets criteria based on obesity and family history, making fasting glucose testing appropriate. Prevention: Weight loss and increased physical activity are the primary strategies to prevent progression to type 2 diabetes mellitus. Treatment: Management is centered on lifestyle modification, with pharmacologic therapy considered in select high-risk cases. Differential: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction presents with symptoms limited to exertion, whereas persistent asthma causes symptoms at rest or with multiple triggers. Insulin resistance and prediabetes are typically asymptomatic and identified through screening in high-risk individuals. This patient’s presentation does not including symptoms or findings consistent with arrhythmias, obstructive sleep apnea, or skin allergies, making the other testing options less appropriate at this time. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: 24-Hour ambulatory ECG monitoring is incorrect. ECG monitoring is used to evaluate arrhythmias causing palpitations or syncope, not isolated exertional respiratory symptoms. Choice C: Methacholine challenge test is incorrect. Methacholine challenge is used when asthma is suspected but not clinically apparent, not when symptoms are clearly limited to exercise. Choice D: Polysomnography is incorrect. Polysomnography evaluates obstructive sleep apnea, which presents with snoring and daytime fatigue rather than isolated exertional wheezing. Choice E: Skin testing for allergens is incorrect. Skin testing for allergens identifies allergic triggers but does not address the need to screen for metabolic disease in this high-risk patient.

Educational Objective: This 14-month-old girl with no acute distress presents with a 3-day history of loose stools and slightly dry buccal mucosa identified on physical examination. The most appropriate next step in management is to recommend use of an oral rehydration solution. Evaluation: Viral gastroenteritis may present with symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and nonbloody diarrhea. Definition: Children with gastroenteritis are at increased risk for volume depletion in comparison to adults. Clinical signs of volume depletion include tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, and prolonged capillary refill. Severe volume depletion secondary to diarrhea is usually accompanied by a significant stool loss of bicarbonate, which, in combination with the hypoperfusion of end organs resulting in lactic acidosis, may result in severe metabolic acidosis. Prevention: The risk for developing viral gastroenteritis may be decreased with proper hand hygiene, infection control measures, and vaccination for rotavirus. Treatment: Oral rehydration therapy is recommended for the treatment of fluid and electrolyte losses caused by mild to moderate gastroenteritis. Oral rehydration therapy is advantageous because of its decreased cost, ease of administration, noninvasive treatment, and ability to be continued at home by caregivers. Most cases of acute viral or bacterial gastroenteritis resolve spontaneously without antibiotic therapy. Differential: This 14-month-old girl has been experiencing loose stools for 5 days and continues to have wet diapers. As she is in no acute distress and has slightly dry buccal mucosa, the most appropriate next step in management for this patient would be recommendation for an oral rehydration solution. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Choice A: Administer intravenous fluids is incorrect. The patient in this case presents with a mild to moderate case of viral gastroenteritis. Intravenous fluids may be indicated when there are signs of severe dehydration, shock, or after failure of attempted treatment with oral rehydration therapy. Choice B: Obtain basic metabolic panel is incorrect. The patient in this case presents with mild signs of dehydration. Recommending use of an oral rehydration solution would be more appropriate. Choice C: Obtain blood culture is incorrect. The patient in this case presents with signs and symptoms of mild to moderate viral gastroenteritis without concern for severe dehydration or shock. Obtaining blood cultures may be indicated if there is concern for bacteremia or sepsis. Choice D: Obtain stool culture is incorrect. This patient most likely is experiencing mild to moderate viral gastroenteritis. A stool culture could be considered if there were signs of bloody diarrhea or persistent diarrhea, in this case, however, recommendation of an oral rehydration solution is more appropriate.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis in a manual laborer with predominantly nighttime hand/wrist pain, numbness, and tingling in the thumb and index finger is compression of the median nerve at the carpal tunnel, also known as carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). The most appropriate initial step in management for this patient with CTS is splinting of the right wrist. Evaluation: CTS presents with pain and paresthesias in the affected thumb, index, and middle finger, often worse at nighttime. The diagnosis is clinical, though when uncertain, nerve conduction studies or electromyography can confirm it. The initial management of mild CTS is wrist splinting. Definition: CTS results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel of the wrist. Finger flexors and the median nerve course through the carpal tunnel, experiencing excessive compression when the wrist is in a flexed position for an extended period. Patients present with hand pain, numbness, and paresthesias in the median nerve dermatomal distribution, sparing the palm. Weakness involving the muscles of the thenar eminence may occur in severe cases. Prevention: Avoiding overuse of the hands and positions of excessive wrist flexion may prevent CTS. Treatment: In mild cases, initial management includes splinting of the wrist. The splint should be worn for as much of the day as tolerated, although particularly at night. In more severe cases, management may include a corticosteroid injection of the carpal tunnel or a carpal tunnel release surgery. Differential: The patient has a mild case of CTS with no hand weakness, and conservative management of splinting should be pursued. The other interventions listed may be appropriate if the diagnosis is uncertain, splinting is ineffective, or the patient presents with a more severe case of CTS, none of which apply to this patient. questions.explanation: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: The physician should initiate a goals-of-care conversation with this patient with life-limiting cardiac illness. Loved ones can assist in honoring the patient’s autonomy by helping them to understand their options and support their decision making. Key Concept: Physicians should initiate goals of care conversations with patients with serious, potentially life-limiting disease. Goals of care conversations should include current and future care preferences, including disposition-related preferences. Explanation: As these decisions are complex and challenging, loved ones commonly assist the medical team in honoring the patient’s autonomy. Social supports can assist the patient in understanding and weighing the options. In a patient unable to physically care for himself, the physician should discuss various levels of postdischarge care, including nursing facilities and home health care, and should also offer hospice services if the disease is terminal. Differential: The patient’s family should wait until the patient expresses his care preferences before providing specific types of assistance (eg, hiring home health care nurses). If the patient lacks decisional capacity regarding his disposition or code status, the family should provide substituted judgment by sharing what the patient would have chosen if capacitated, another way of honoring the patient’s autonomy. The patient’s family should wait until the patient expresses his care preferences before providing specific types of assistance. Choice B: Expressing the patient’s wishes is inappropriate. This patient is cognizant and should be allowed and encouraged to express his own wishes. Choice E: Making decisions for the patient is inappropriate. If the patient lacks decisional capacity regarding his disposition or code status, the family should provide substituted judgment by sharing what the patient would have chosen if capacitated. Educational Objective: Asbestosis is the most likely cause of this patient’s pleuritic chest pain, cough, night sweats, thickened and calcified pleura, and associated pleural effusion. Asbestosis likely occurred in this patient as a result of chronic asbestos exposure during his career installing insulation. Key Concept: Asbestosis results from chronic asbestos exposure, with high-risk occupations including plumbers, pipefitters, steamfitters, electricians, insulation workers, carpenters, and general laborers. Explanation: Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis that results from inhalation of asbestos fibers leading to inflammation and fibrosis of the alveoli and pulmonary interstitium. Patients may be asymptomatic or develop chronic pulmonary disease characterized by a chronic cough and dyspnea associated with progressive pulmonary fibrosis. Physical examination may disclose pulmonary crackles, digital clubbing, and signs of pulmonary hypertension, such as parasternal heave. Characteristic imaging findings include bilateral infiltrates with a lower lung predominance, calcified pleural plaques, rounded atelectasis, and pleural effusions. Differential: Calcified pleural plaques with associated pleural effusions are pathognomonic for asbestosis. While these other risk factors predispose this patient to a variety of health issues, exposure to asbestos is the cause of asbestosis. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Age is incorrect. Age increases the risk for a variety of ailments, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes mellitus. Age is not directly correlated to the development of asbestosis. Choice C: Chronic cannabis use is incorrect. Cannabis has not been definitively proven to increase the risk for chronic pulmonary or cardiovascular disease. While it can exacerbate pre-existing pneumonia and cause airway irritation, it does not cause asbestosis. Choice D: Mold exposure is incorrect. Mold exposure can be associated with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which is an inflammatory condition of the lungs in response to environmental irritants. Chest x-ray will classically show bilateral infiltrates, not calcified pleural plaques with pleural effusions. Choice E: International travel to Vietnam is incorrect. Travel to places where tuberculosis exposure is prevalent, such as Vietnam, amongst other places, increases the risk for reactivation tuberculosis in patients with latent exposure. However, tuberculosis presents with infiltrates and cavitary lesions on chest x-ray, rather than the findings seen in this patient.
